o: A prefixed plexus (C4-C8) occurs in about 10%

In about 10 percent the brachial plexus is prefixed (C4 to C8), and in about 10 percent postfixed (C6 to T2).
The root levels of injuries shift accordingly.
The divisions lie behind the clavicle

The trunks divide into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle; the roots and trunks are above it and the cords below.
So clavicle fractures can affect the divisions.
The lateral cord is formed from the lower anterior division

The medial cord is formed from the lower anterior division. The lateral cord is formed from the upper and middle anterior divisions.
All three posterior divisions form the posterior cord.
The cords embrace the first part of the axillary artery

The cords embrace the second part of the axillary artery, behind pectoralis minor, not the first part.
They are named by their relation to it.

questions.s: Branches from the roots and trunks (Last's):
o: The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) passes behind the roots

The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) passes back through scalenus medius, behind the roots, to supply the rhomboids.
It runs with the dorsal scapular artery.
The nerve to subclavius passes in front of the roots

The nerve to subclavius (C5, C6) runs down in front of the roots and the subclavian vessels.
It may carry an accessory phrenic branch.
The long thoracic nerve passes in front of the roots

The long thoracic nerve passes behind the roots, not in front.
It then descends on serratus anterior.
The suprascapular nerve arises from the lateral cord

The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk, not the lateral cord.
It is the only branch of a trunk.
The thoracodorsal nerve is C6, 7, 8

The thoracodorsal nerve (C6, C7, C8) arises from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi.
It is preserved in axillary surgery when possible.
The ulnar nerve is C7, 8, T1

The ulnar nerve is C8 and T1 from the medial cord, plus C7 fibres from the lateral cord.
So its root value is C7, C8, T1.
The axillary nerve arises from the lateral cord

The axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord, not the lateral cord.
With the radial nerve.
The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the posterior cord

The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the medial cord, not the posterior cord.
It is T1.
The long thoracic nerve supplies the lowest four digitations of serratus anterior from C7

The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior segmentally: C5 to the first two digitations, C6 to the next two and C7 to the lowest four.
Lesions cause winging of the scapula.
Pectoralis major is supplied by all five segments of the plexus

Pectoralis major is the only muscle supplied by all five segments of the brachial plexus.
C5 to T1 via the two pectoral nerves.
The nerve to subclavius never carries phrenic fibres

The nerve to subclavius may carry an accessory phrenic contribution.
So "never" is wrong.
The dorsal scapular nerve supplies latissimus dorsi

The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and often levator scapulae, not latissimus dorsi.
Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.
Its first part has one branch

The first part of the axillary artery has one branch, the superior thoracic.
The number of branches matches the part number.
Its third part has three branches

The third part has three branches: the subscapular and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
The largest branch is the subscapular.
The lateral thoracic artery arises from the third part

The lateral thoracic artery arises from the second part, with the thoracoacromial.
The second part has two branches.
It becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of pectoralis minor

The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major, not pectoralis minor.
Pectoralis minor only divides it into parts.
It passes through the quadrangular space

The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
It winds round the surgical neck.
Its posterior branch supplies teres minor

The posterior branch of the axillary nerve supplies teres minor and becomes the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.
The anterior branch supplies most of deltoid.
It lies below the posterior circumflex humeral vessels

In the quadrangular space the axillary nerve lies above the posterior circumflex humeral vessels, close to the capsule.
So inferior dislocation stretches it.
It supplies the skin over the upper half of deltoid

The cutaneous branch of the axillary nerve supplies the skin over the lower half of deltoid (the regimental badge area), not the upper half.
The upper half is supraclavicular (C4).

questions.s: Spaces in the posterior axillary wall:
o: The quadrangular space is bounded medially by the long head of triceps

The quadrangular space is bounded by teres minor above, teres major below, the long head of triceps medially and the humerus laterally.
It transmits the axillary nerve.
The triangular space (lower) transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels

The lower triangular space (triangular interval), below teres major, transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii vessels.
Lateral to the long head of triceps.
The quadrangular space is bounded above by teres major

The quadrangular space is bounded above by teres minor (with subscapularis in front); teres major forms its lower boundary.
"Minor above, major below."
The circumflex scapular artery passes through the quadrangular space

The circumflex scapular artery passes through the upper triangular space, between subscapularis/teres minor, teres major and the long head, medial to the long head.
The quadrangular space is lateral.
It pierces coracobrachialis

The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, supplying it, then runs between biceps and brachialis.
It supplies all three flexors of the arm.
It continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm

Beyond the elbow it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
It supplies the lateral forearm skin.
It is the sole supply of brachialis

Brachialis also receives a lateral branch from the radial nerve, so the musculocutaneous is not its sole supply.
A dual supply.
It pierces the deep fascia medial to the biceps tendon

The nerve pierces the deep fascia lateral to the biceps tendon, not medial.
The median nerve lies medial to the tendon.
It usually supplies no muscle above the elbow

The median nerve usually supplies no muscle above the elbow, unless there is a high branch to pronator teres.
Its branches are in the forearm and hand.
It passes between the two heads of pronator teres

The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres, then under the fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis.
Both are sites of compression.
In the carpal tunnel it lies medial to the FDS tendons

In the carpal tunnel the median nerve lies lateral to the FDS tendon to the middle finger and medial to flexor carpi radialis, not medial to the FDS tendons.
It is superficial and lateral.
The palmar cutaneous branch arises within the carpal tunnel

The palmar cutaneous branch arises just above the flexor retinaculum, not within the carpal tunnel.
So it is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.s: Hand muscles and the median nerve (Last's):
o: Flexor pollicis brevis has the most variable innervation of any muscle

Last's says flexor pollicis brevis has the most variable innervation of any muscle: median, ulnar or both.
So thenar wasting varies.
Opponens pollicis usually has a double supply

Opponens pollicis usually has a double supply, median and ulnar.
A Last's point.
The median nerve supplies all four lumbricals

The median nerve supplies the two lateral lumbricals; the ulnar supplies the two medial ones.
Not all four.
The medial and lateral branches of the median nerve arise in the forearm

The medial and lateral branches of the median nerve arise in the carpal tunnel, not in the forearm.
The recurrent branch arises from the lateral branch.
It gives no branches in the arm

The ulnar nerve gives no branches in the arm.
Its first branch is to FCU at the elbow.
It pierces the medial intermuscular septum in the lower third of the arm

The ulnar nerve pierces the medial intermuscular septum in the lower third of the arm with the superior ulnar collateral artery.
It then passes behind the medial epicondyle.
It passes through the cubital fossa

The ulnar nerve does not pass through the cubital fossa. The fossa contains the median nerve, brachial artery and biceps tendon.
The ulnar nerve is behind the medial epicondyle.
Its C7 fibres usually come from the middle trunk

In more than 95 percent the C7 fibres of the ulnar nerve come from the lateral cord, not the middle trunk.
They supply FCU.

questions.s: The ulnar nerve at the wrist and hand (Last's):
o: It divides into superficial and deep branches on the flexor retinaculum

The ulnar nerve divides into superficial and deep branches on the flexor retinaculum, beside the pisiform.
In Guyon's canal.
Its superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis

The superficial branch of the ulnar nerve supplies palmaris brevis and the skin of the medial one and a half digits.
It is the only motor fibre of the superficial branch.
Its C7 fibres supply the interossei

Last's says the C7 fibres of the ulnar nerve form the branch to FCU in the forearm, not the supply to the interossei.
The interossei are C8 and T1.
Its deep branch passes medial to the hook of hamate without contacting it

The deep branch of the ulnar nerve lies on the hook of hamate (curving around it), and can be compressed there.
So it does contact it.
It leaves the axilla through the triangular space

The radial nerve leaves the axilla through the lower triangular space with the profunda brachii vessels.
Then it enters the spiral groove.
The ulnar collateral nerve is the first branch to the medial head of triceps

The first branch of the radial nerve to the medial head of triceps runs with the ulnar nerve and is called the ulnar collateral nerve.
A Last's term.
It pierces the medial intermuscular septum

The radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, not the medial.
The ulnar nerve pierces the medial one.
The posterior interosseous nerve supplies extensor carpi radialis longus

The radial nerve itself supplies ECRL before giving off the posterior interosseous nerve.
The PIN supplies ECRB and supinator onward.
Sensory loss is usually a coin-shaped area over the first dorsal interosseous

Because of overlap from the median and ulnar nerves, radial sensory loss is usually only a coin-sized area over the first dorsal interosseous.
The autonomous zone.
The posterior interosseous nerve passes between the two layers of supinator

The posterior interosseous nerve passes between the superficial and deep layers of supinator, where it can be compressed.
Radial tunnel syndrome.
Sensory loss covers the whole dorsum of the radial 3.5 digits

Radial sensory loss is much smaller than the whole dorsum of the radial three and a half digits, because of overlap.
Only a small patch is reliably anaesthetic.
The PIN supplies brachioradialis

Brachioradialis is supplied by the radial nerve itself, not the posterior interosseous nerve.
It works in PIN palsy.
The flexor retinaculum attaches radially to the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium

Radially the flexor retinaculum attaches to the scaphoid tubercle and the ridge of the trapezium.
The FCR tendon runs in a groove in the trapezium.
It attaches medially to the pisiform and hook of hamate

Medially it attaches to the pisiform and the hook of hamate.
These four bony points form the carpal arch.
EPL forms the radial boundary of the snuffbox

Extensor pollicis longus forms the ulnar (medial) boundary of the snuffbox. Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis form the radial boundary.
EPL hooks round Lister's tubercle.
The cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia with the medial pectoral nerve

The cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia with the lateral pectoral nerve, not the medial.
The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor.
The lower subscapular nerve supplies teres major

The lower subscapular nerve supplies the lower part of subscapularis and teres major.
Both from the posterior cord.
The thoracodorsal nerve enters the deep surface of latissimus dorsi

The thoracodorsal nerve runs down the posterior axillary wall to enter the deep surface of latissimus dorsi.
It accompanies the thoracodorsal artery.
The thoracodorsal nerve lies behind the thoracodorsal artery as it descends

As it descends, the thoracodorsal nerve comes to lie in front of the thoracodorsal artery, not behind it.
A Last's detail.
Latissimus dorsi developed in the flexor compartment

Latissimus dorsi developed in the extensor (dorsal) compartment of the limb, which is why it is supplied by the posterior cord.
A limb muscle that has spread onto the back.

questions.s: Cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm (Last's):
o: The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm runs with the axillary vein

The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm runs down medial to the axillary vein.
It supplies the medial arm.
The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm runs between axillary artery and vein

The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm runs between the axillary artery and vein, then pierces the deep fascia with the basilic vein.
It supplies the medial forearm.
The medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm overlap widely at the anterior axial line

Last's says the medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm meet without overlap at the anterior axial line.
That is the nature of an axial line.
The posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm arises from the ulnar nerve

The posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm arises from the radial nerve, not the ulnar.
It leaves the radial nerve in the spiral groove.
